messages.author: 9498334c020f9a13
messages.subject: ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
Hi everyone,

Since this is my first post I have to thank the Stan developers for producing such a useful tool!

I need to evaluate integrals where the limits of integration are parameters, not data.  I would prefer to use Stan's ODE solver but it only can return solutions at data values.  Is there a workaround?

Thanks,
Alex

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
You're talking about solving ODEs? We don't actually have a simple
integrator built in.

The only way I could think to deal with this would be hacking it
with parameters defining the offset of times inside the ODE itself.
I don't see a way to do it cleanly. You can already think of initial
conditions as being done that way under the hood.

- Bob

messages.author: 9498334c020f9a13
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
Hi Bob,

It seems that a leapfrog integrator is available to solve ODEs.  I was able to define a differential equation "friedmann" in the function block, and then evaluate the function at several data values using

  luminosity_distance_obs <- integrate_ode(friedmann, r0, z0, zs_obs, theta, x_r, x_i);

where zs_obs is declared in the data block: this works fine.  Now I want to evaluate the function for missing data declared in the parameter block but the API does not allow this.

There is no way to do this cleanly?

Alex

messages.author: 9498334c020f9a13
messages.subject: Re: ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
I enclose a redacted version of my stan code if it helps.

Alex

functions{
  // differential equation we want to solve is dz/H = dr/sqrt(1-kr2)
  // H^2/H_0^2 = Omega_R a-4 + Omega_M a-3 + Omega_k a-2 + Omega_L
  real[] friedmann(real z,
          real[] r,
          real[] theta,
          real[] x_r,
          int[] i_r){
    real H2;
    real drdz[1];
    real omega_k;
    omega_k <- (1-theta[1]-theta[2]);
    H2 <- theta[1]*(1+z)^3 + theta[2]+ omega_k*(1+z)^2;
    drdz[1] <- sqrt((1-fabs(omega_k)/omega_k*r[1])/H2);
    return drdz;
  }

data{
  int<lower=1> N_sn;
  int<lower=0> N_s_obs;
  int<lower=0> N_s_mis;

  real<lower=0, upper=2> zs_obs[N_s_obs];
}

transformed data {

  // data needed for solution for the ode including the zeropoints for z and r
  real x_r[0];
  int x_i[0];

  real r0[1];
  real z0;

  r0[1] <- 0;
  z0 <- 0;
}

parameters{
  // cosmology parameters
  real <lower=0,upper=1> theta[2];

  // missing data spectroscopy
  real<lower=0, upper=1.5> zs_mis[N_s_mis];
 }

transformed parameters{
  real luminosity_distance_obs[N_s_obs,1];
  real luminosity_distance_mis[N_s_mis,1];

  // luminosity distance
  // this works fine!
luminosity_distance_obs <- integrate_ode(friedmann, r0, z0, zs_obs, theta, x_r, x_i);

// would like to do this but fails because zs_mis is a parameter
  luminosity_distance_mis <- integrate_ode(friedmann, r0, z0, zs_mis, theta, x_r, x_i);

}

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
I’m not sure what you think the model will do here — you have
no distribution over observation times (neither prior or likelihood)
so there’s nothing for you to infer.  

Unless luminosity_distance_mis are actual observations without
observation times, in which case you might be able to hack
something using the fact that the initial conditions can be
uncertain.  Still, that’s going to be a tricky model and you
probably won’t get great results.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
Right --- there's definitely no clean way to do this.
We set that up on purpose because in all the cases we know of,
the times for solutions are observation times that are known.

What I was suggesting is similar to what Michael was suggesting.
If you have a time t (?) that's uncertain, then you need to
add in a parameter t_offset and replace t in the diff eq with
(t + t_offset). Then you can do inference on the offset. If
it's multiple times of uncertainty, then it's going to require
a pretty ugly hack.

- Bob

messages.author: 9498334c020f9a13
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE evaluated at parameter values
parts:
Thanks for the response.  Indeed it seems that the internal integrator is not meant for use outside of its core job of probing the pdf surface.  My usage is to transform parameters.

I have made a hack solution, defining a grid in transformed data, calculating the integrals on that grid, and then cubic splining the solution to the parameter values.  Good enough for my current needs.

Alex
